title: Growing Caucasian spinach
subtitle: A shade-tolerant climbing perennial grown for its spinach-like spring shoots.
excerpt: Caucasian spinach is a perennial climber that produces spinach-like shoots in spring and early summer. It is one of the few edible plants that thrives in deep shade and, once established, is almost entirely self-managing.
sourceNotes: Species information from Martin Crawford, Creating a Forest Garden (2010). Plants For A Future database (pfaf.org). UK cultivation notes from Agroforestry Research Trust.

glossaryTerms.definition: A climbing plant that dies back to the ground each winter and regrows from the roots each spring. Unlike woody climbers such as wisteria or climbing roses, herbaceous climbers need no permanent framework support — they can scramble each year up the same structure as they regrow.

content.text: from the Caucasus region. The young shoots emerging in spring are cooked and eaten exactly like spinach. It is unusual among edible plants in growing well in deep shade, making it valuable in north-facing gardens, under trees, and in a forest garden ground-cover role.

Caucasian spinach is available as seed and occasionally as pot-grown plants from specialist perennial vegetable suppliers. Sow seed in pots in March to April. Germination takes two to three weeks. The plant establishes slowly in the first year but grows vigorously from the second.

Plant in partial or full shade. Full sun in a dry summer causes the leaves to scorch. Provide a structure to climb: wire mesh on a fence, a trellis, or an old shrub. The stems reach 2 to 3 m in a good season and twine up whatever support is available.

Harvest the young shoots as they emerge in March and April, when they are 10 to 20 cm long. Steam or stir-fry like spinach. By May and June the stems become tougher and less palatable. From July the plant is climbing and producing flowers; at this point harvest is largely over for the year.

Cut the whole plant to the ground in October or November after the stems die back. Mulch the crown with a thick layer of leaves or compost to protect it over winter. In a sheltered garden with mild winters it needs no protection at all.
